ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Thrust to Marine Exports from Tamil Nadu by MPEDA  
*281. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased 
to state: 
(a)  whether Marine Product Export Development Authority (MPEDA) is giving sufficient 
thrust to marine exports from Tamil Nadu; 
(b)  if so, what is the quantum of export of marine products from Tamil Nadu in 2006-07 
and the current year upto 31 st December, 2007; 
(c)  whether it is a fact that the MPEDA has not surveye d the full potential of marine 
fisheries of Tuticorin and other marine areas; and 
(d)  what steps are proposed to formulate a special scheme to encourage local people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY 
OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid ori the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a)  Yes, Sir. 
(b)  The item-wise export details from Tamil Nadu in 200 6-07 and 2007-08 up to 31st 
December, 2007 are given in the Statement I. (see below) 
(c)  MPEDA has conducted a survey in all the States including Tamil Nadu for exploiting 
the full potential of marine fisheries in these areas. Based on this, an action plan has been 
drawn up both for export production as well as promotion. There are three offices of MPEDA 
in Tamil Nadu, one each in Chennai and Tuticorin and the third at Thanjavur mandated to 
look after exports. 
(d)  MPEDA closely works with the primary producers and exporters to enhance export 
production, improvement of quality, sustainable aspects of fisheries, etc. in the coastal areas. 
MPEDA's field offices work with various establishments in the State to encourage the local 
people. The newly formed Societies namely, National Centre for Sustainable Aquaculture 
(NaCSA) and Network for Fish Quality Mangement & Sustainable Fishing (NETFISH) 
constituted under the aegis of MPEDA work with prim ary producers like farmers and 
fishermen in increasing their capacity to meet the growing challenges in export production, 
quality aspects, supply chain improvement, sustainability, etc.

SHRI D. RAJA: Sir, I am happy that the Minister has tried to give some answer. But there 
is a general impression that the Marine Product Export Development Authority (MPEDA) is 
not doing much. Tamil Nadu has a very vast coastlin e, yet there has not been significant 
growth in the export of marine products. I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to 
what are the reasons for the poor performance of th e MPEDA in ensuring that our exports 
are value-added, and not just frozen shrimp or fish . Why is the MPEDA not concentrating 
on improving exports? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the impression that the MPEDA is not doing enough for 
promoting export is not right. In the last three years there has been significant turn around in 
our export performance. It used to stagnate throughout the nineties at about 1.2 to 1.3 billion 
dollars. But in 2005-06, it was 1.6 billion dollars. Last year, it reached 1.8 billion dollars. 
This year we hope to close with an export of about 2 billion dollars, so, in the last three 
years, there has been a significant turn around in the export performance. I agree that the 
export performance could be better. But there are s evere problems in the fact that almost 
54 per cent of our exports is constituted by shrimp  alone. We need to diversify away from 
this dependence on shrimp. That is precisely the reason why the Tenth Plan allocation for the 
MPEDA was Rs. 200 crore, while the Eleventh Plan allocation is Rs. 450 Crores. It is very 
significant step up. You will see results during the Eleventh Plan period. We have issued a 
vision document for the first time for marine product exports and we hope to reach an export 
target of 4 billion dollars by the year 2012. 
SHRI D. RAJA: Sir, I would like to put my supplementary in relation to my last question. 
I understand that the MPEDA is favouring foreign Tuna companies of the USA and Europe. 
I would like the Minister to tell us as to why the MPEDA is supporting the orders of the 
Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, which is a body consi sting of all European countries and 
the American countries. Only about seven Indian Oce an countries are there. The European 
and American countries have almost 5,000 tuna boats, while India has only a small number 
of boats about twenty. The MPEDA is supporting the IOTC and wants Indians to surrender 
all the rights. 

Oral Answers [19 MARCH 2008] to Questions 3  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
SHRI D. RAJA: Sir, I must tell the hon. Minister also that the fishermen federations have 
represented to the Government. There is an adverse impact because of the free-trade 
agreement. We have free-trade agreement with the Eu ropean Union; we have free-trade 
agreement with USA; we have free-trade agreement with ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
SHRI D. RAJA: This is for the question, Sir. So, there is an adverse impact due to free-
trade agreement. There is also the problem of coastal zones. Fishermen have asked to scrap 
the recommendations made by ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Raja, please put your question. 
SHRI D. RAJA: I want the hon. Minister to respond t o all these issues because .. 
.(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Only one supplementary question please. 
SHRI D. RAJA: Sir, this is related to my last question. How is the Government going to 
promote and protect the interests of the local fish ing community? Unless the Government 
protects their interest, how can our economy thrive on? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the hon. Member is sufferi ng from series of 
misapprehensions, which are absolutely not true. As far as tuna is concerned, today, in our 
export basket of about 1.8 billion dollars, tuna's export is only about 20 million dollars. The 
Indian Ocean Tuna Commission is an inter-Government body of 28 Indian Ocean countries. 
This is headquartered at Seychelles. India is a member of this body. We need to increase the 
contribution of tuna to our exports. We need to diversify away from shrimp. Our plan is to 
reach a tuna export of about 500 million dollars by the year 2012. Tuna is a highly complicated, 
highly technology intensive type of fisheries unlike shrimp which is, comparatively, easier. 
We need to get technology from abroad. That is what we are trying to do. We are converting 
the existing fishing into long liners for tuna. There is, absolutely, no question of depending 
on somebody else for tuna. I also want to inform th e hon. Member that tuna is a highly 
migratory species offish. If we do not catch our tuna in our waters, this tuna migrates and it 
gets caught in by countries, like Thailand and it g ets attributed to countries of South East 
Asia. We need to move into tuna more aggressively than we have been. 
Sir, as far as Free Trade Agreements are concerned,  I would like to inform the hon. 
Member that there is no Free Trade Agreement with A merica. As far as the Free Trade 
Agreement with the European Union is concerned, negotiations have started. Two rounds of 
negotiations have taken place. And the hon. Minister for Commerce has assured the Chief 
Ministers of Kerala and other coastal States that the interests of the fishing community will 
be taken into account fully when negotiating the fi nal agreement. There is no question of 
opening our markets to foreign fish products and sacrificing the interests of our own fishermen. 
. ..(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Thank you, Mr. Raja. You have had your say. Shri Malaisamy. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. The Minister has said in his reply 
that he has made a thorough survey about the potent iality. I am inclined to know from the 
hon. Minister and hope that he will answer this wit h his thoroughness he used to. I would 
like to know whether any potentiality study has bee n done in and around the Katchateevu 
area. 

4 Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put the question. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: I would like to know whether enough potentiality is available in 
and around Katchateevu or not. If available, can it  be created by some device through the 
migration of various kinds of fish, etc. and brought them to our Indian territory? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the new thrust area for fisheries for tuna, particularly, is 
going to be the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which has about 25-30 per cent of India's 
tuna potential. As far as Inland aquaculture is con cerned, the focus States are going to be 
Gujarat and Maharashtra which have significant underdeveloped brackish water aquaculture 
potential. As far as Katchateevu is concerned, Sir,  I am not in a position to answer this 
question. But, in view of the importance of Katchateevu to the hon. Member. I will get back 
to him very soon on this. 
PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. Si r, the hon. Minister is a very 
efficient Minister and he has given good answer. But, in the answer itself there is a question. 
He said that our tuna export is very small when com pared with the total potential we are 
having. Sir, we have, hardly, 20 vessels. When there is so much of scope and potential. I am 
surprised to see that you are not doing anything. Let me put the question. Sir, the reasons is 
that... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put the question. 
PROF. RJ. KURIEN: They are subsevient to the IODTC about which my friend. Shri D. 
Raja mentioned. I would like to know, especially, from the hon. Minister what the Government 
is doing to ensure that our full potential of tuna is caught and exported. I would also like to 
know, specifically, what the MPEDA, which is meant for promoting this, is doing in this 
area. 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, for the first time, a perspective plan for tuna fishing has 
been prepared. This was released in Port Blair just  two months ago. I will be glad to share 
the copy of this perspective plan for tuna with the hon. Member. I mentioned it earlier and I 
would like to repeat that our plan is to reach an e xport level of about $ 500 million in the 
next five years. It is possible. The main focus of tuna fishing is going to be Andamans, but, 
there is also substantial potential for tuna in Vis akhapatnam and Tuticorin as well. Tuna is 
going to be the thrust area for the MPEDA. I would like to reiterate that it is highly technology-
intensive. It is going to call for new investments in fishing harbours, in long liners, etc. And, 
we are in the process of bringing about these changes. I would like to assure the hon. Member 
that in this process, the maximum priority is going  to be given to conversion of existing 
fishing vessels into tuna liners. There is no question of getting tuna liners from abroad. 
SHRJ S.S. AHLUWALIA: Sir, again and again, the hon. Minister, in his reply, is saying 
that catching tuna fish is a very technology-intens ive area. As I understand, we have got 
about 1,50,000 nautical miles area in the EEZ and w e are not commercially exploiting that 
area totally. Tuna has a good potential in the worl d market, especially in Japan. But, 
unfortunately, the foreign trawlers are using a special type of light below their trawlers which 
attracts tuna fish towards them. As the hon. Minister said right now, tuna is a migratory fish 
and, naturally, it is attracted by the foreign traw lers. Why is the Indian Government or the 
MPEDA not buying that type of technology and that t ype of trawlers to catch tuna in our 
areas, or, to attract tuna from the other areas to our areas? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, as I have explained, MPEDA  has got in to tuna for the 
first time only in the last four or five months. We had prepared a detailed perspective plan

which I will be able to share with the hon. Members very soon and even today. And, it is our 
intention to do all that we can to enable domestic industry to benefit from diversification in 
to tuna. It requires long liners, it requires processing on-board and the hon. Member is right 
when he says that there is a substantial potential for export of tuna, particularly, to Japan and 
South-East Asia, which we have not exploited. I believe, Sir, that this is one very important 
area as far as marine products are concerned, the movement away from our dependence on

6 Oral Answers [RAJAYA SABHA] to Questions  
(c) In order to improve and adopt better marketing techniques, the following steps have 
been taken by MPEDA: 
(i) Participation in major international fairs worl d-wide to strengthen the existing 
markets and capture new markets. MPEDA participated  in 7 international fairs 
during 2006-07, and in 8 major fairs held in Japan,  USA, Brazil, EU, China, 
Russia, etc. during the current year. 
(ii) Advertisements in selected international and reputed commercial magazines and 
journals published from UK, USA, Japan, etc. to publicize India's fishery resources, 
infra-structural developments and capabilities in p roducing and exporting value 
added products. 
(iii) Organising buyer seller meets during the major international seafood fairs. A major 
market promotion event was organized in conjunction with the European Seafood 
Exposition, 2007 at Brussels. 
(iv) Organising the Biennial India International Seafood show in major cities in India 
in association with Seafood Exporters Association of India. The 16th Fair in the 
series was held in Kochi from 8-10th February 2008. Events such as these provide 
the buyers and sellers an opportunity to evolve sui table strategies for forging 
trade relationships for mutual benefits. 
(v) Engagement of a reputed professional agency as a consultant to promote Indian 
Seafood in overseas retail markets like EU, USA and Japan and to create a brand 
image for Indian Sea food in major overseas super M arkets. 
(vi) Extension of Developmental Assistance to boost  the export of Ornamental 
Aquarium Fishes from India enabling an exporter to get a Developmental 
Assistance of 10% of FOB value of exports subject to a maximum of Rs. 3 lakh 
per exporter per year. 
(vii) Thrust to export of tuna fish and fishery products, by conversion of vessels, training 
in tuna longlining and on board handling of fish. A  special delegation was also 
deputed to visit Japan to strengthen marketing ties. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir; there is a need to upgrade the level of skills, knowledge and capability 
of the staff of MPEDA frequently. 
MPEDA is taking the following steps to upgrade knowledge and skill base of its human 
resources:— 
(i) MPEDA has signed an MOU with IIM Ahmedabad to c onduct a study on its 
Performance appraisal system with the aim of revamp ing its organizational 
structure. 
(ii) Organizing short term HR training programmes on the marine sector for MPEDA 
officials through the faculty members from reputed management institutions like, 
CIFNET, IIFT, IIM, etc. 
(iii) Organizing field orientation training programmes as per the need of the officials 
to improve their knowledge base in concerned subjects and depute them to other 
institutions for participating in the training programmes related to their relevant 
subject. 

Oral Answers [19 MARCH 2008] to Questions 7 
(iv) Leadership training. 
(v) Frequent, intensive in-house orientation training for the officers. 
(vi) Training of officers in latest technologies in aquaculture in various national and 
international institutes. 
(vii) Sponsoring officials to attend international seminars/symposia etc. for updating 
their knowledge levels. 
(viii) Besides organizing in-house trainings, MPEDA is deputing its officers abroad for 
various trainings/seminars/workshops being organize d by international 
organizations like Euopean Commission, US FDA, NMFS , for acquiring and 
enhancing their technical competency. 
(f) MPEDA has prepared Vision document outlining the strategic roadmap for the marine 
products export sector. Among the interventions envisaged are: 
(i) Expansion and diversification of aquaculture. 
(ii) Exploration of our unexploited deep sea fishing resources, particularly tuna. 
(iii) Substantive increase in value addition. 
(iv) Making India a processing hub.

8 Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
SHRI JAIRMAN RAMESH. Sir, the location of MPEDA in Cochin has in no way deterred 
MPEDA's activities in other States. I would like to inform the hon. member that out of a total 
export of about $ 1.8 billion, Tamil Nadu accounts for about $ 450 million, Kerala itself 
accounts for about $ 350 million and Andhra Pradesh accounts for about $ 270 million. So, 
it is not true to say that the contribution of Kerala is miniscule. In fact, the centre of the sea-
food processing industry is Cochin. That is one of the reasons why MPEDA was located in 
Cochin. Sir, we are taking a lot of efforts to develop the fisheries industry in other States. As 
I mentioned earlier, as far as inland aquaculture i s concerned, the two new States that are 
being taken up are Gujarat and Maharashtra, which have about 40 per cent of India's potential 
and which has not been exploited. As far as Andhra Pradesh is concerned, this Government 
has'located the National Fisheries Development Board in Hyderabad and as far as MPEDA 
is concerned, we have taken up a number of measures  to build up testing laboratories, 
hatcheries, and a variety of other institutional mechanisms to promote fishery exports from 
Andhra Pradesh. In fact, Sir, the hon. Member would  be pleased to know that just four 
months ago, we have located the National Centre for Sustainable Aquaculture in Kakinada, 
and, if I recall right, sir, Kakinada was last in Andhra Pradesh. ...(Interruptions)... Mr. Sitaram 
Yechury is from Kakinada. ...(Interruptions)...  
SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Sir, with your permission, I would say that the country has 
had the experience of Mohammad Bin Tuglak once. So, please do not ask about shifting of 
its headquarters from one place to another.

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, strengthening  the MPEDA is one 
important aspect. Instead of keeping restrictions on the functioning of the organisation, we 
need to improve the human resource there in the organisation. This is one aspect. Secondly, 
you have talked about making India a processing hub. What are the steps taken by the Ministry 
for improving the processing units? And the third t hing is related to improving the 
infrastructrue in Lakshadweep regarding tuna fish. We had been to that area. A very small 
unit is there. Is there any proposal with the Government of India to improve the infrastructure 
there? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, as far as processing is co ncerned, we have substantial 
processing capacity, but, for a variety of reasons,  unfortunately, the capacity utlisation has 
not been more than twenty-five to thirty per cent. We are taking steps to ensure that India 
emerges as a processing hub. One of the proposals that is under examination in the Ministry 
of Agriculture—since we are not the relevant Ministry here — is to allow Indian processing

industry access to imported vanami fish which will be processed here and we export it 
through some value addition. These are proposals that are under examination for the fuller 
utilisation of our processing sector. 
Sir, as far as Lakshadweep is concerned, there is s ome tuna activity going on in 
Lakshadweep. But as I mentioned in my earlier answer. Sir, almost twenty-five to thirty per 
cent of India's tuna potential is around the EEZ, the Exclusive Economic Zone in the Andaman  
and Nicobar Islands and that is going to constitute the focus of our activity. But if investments 
are required to upscale the contribution of Lakshad weep, MPEDA would be prepared to 
make these investments. 
SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: Sir, the hon. Minister has been kind enough to say what 
the Government of lndia is doing as far as improving the conditions for promoting exports 
of fish in Andhra. The specific question I would like .to put is this. Is there any possibility of 
opening a branch office of MPEDA at Visakhapatnam? Sir, why I am saying this is because 
we don't want to shift the main office. The House should understand that there is no question 
of any demand for shifting the main office. But we want a branch office of MPEDA at 
Visakhapatnam, because, in the whole coast, from Bapatla to Visakhapatnam, there is a huge 
activity. ...(Interruptions)... Would the hon. Minister kindly answer it? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, I think the hon. Member should be aware that there is a 
very substantial MPEDA presence already in Andhra P radesh. 
SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: Sir, we want an office. In wh at way the 'presence' is 
....(Interruptions)...  
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, we have offices in Andhra Pradesh. ...(Interruptions)... 
Sir, I would like the hon. Member to be aware that there are offices in Andhra Pradesh. 
There are officers in Andhra Pradesh. We have located the National Centre for Sustainable 
Aquaculture, which is run by MPEDA in Kakinada. The hon. Minister of State for Defence 
was present when this centre was inaugurated. So, we have very substantial offices. We have 
very substantial officers. We have very substantial investments. And, as I have mentioned, 
Sir, day-after-tomorrow I myself am going to Visakhapatnam to have a further discussion on 
what more we can do, specifically for the State of Andhra Pradesh. 
SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: That must include the branch office also.

Applying strategy of Punjab and Mizoram to wipe out  militancy 
in other States 
*287.      SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR:tt 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether Government has drawn some basic conclusions  from Punjab and Mizoram 
from where militancy has been wiped out; 
(b)  if so, whether the success of security forces in these States reflected the need by other 
States to adopt a strategy that aimed at securing t he confidence and support of the local 
population; and 
(c)  whether such a course of action will be charted by the Centre and popularized amongst 
insurgency-inflicted States to begin with? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) to (c) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (c) The Government has been adopting a multi -pronged approach and strategy to 
deal with the situation in areas affected by militancy and insurgency, etc., which, inter-alia, 
includes action on the security front, focus on acc elerated development, goad governance 
and measures for building confidence in the local population, including efforts to draw those 
involved in the militancy/insurgency into the mains tream. The experience gathered in the 
process of countering militancy and insurgency, etc., in different areas, is constantly used to 
formulate and calibrate strategies, plan and policies in this regard. 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: Sir, the hon. Ministe r has talked about the 
Home Department's multi-pronged approach and strategy to deal with various situations. I 
would like to say that insurgency-inflicted States require more security forces. Whenever 
there are elections in the neighbouring States of Meghalaya, Manipur, Nagaland and Tripura, 
some security forces are shifted from Assam to those States. As a result, for lack of adequate 
security forces, many people die due to attack by terrorists. In Karbi Anglong, Tinsukia and

Dhemaji we have seen it happening regularly. Though the Government's policy has already 
been stated, will they think about the matter? Will the Home Ministry consider this and not 
shift security forces from Assam to those States whenever there is election? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, 1 am very sorry to say that the forces which are available 
with the State Governments are not being used in the manner in which they should be used. 
And, every time an incident takes place, the Union Government is asked to send some more 
forces. We have very limited number of forces with us. In one of the replies 1 had explained 
to this House that out of eight lakh men and office rs with us, nearly six lakh forces are 
deployed at the international borders. And out of the remaining Forces, we have to send the 
Forces to the State Governments and as it happens to be a State subject, it is expected that 
the State Government should raise their own Forces and then deploy them. They should also 
fill in the vacancies, which are there. I am very sorry to inform this House that some of the 
States are having as many vacancies as 30 per cent of their Forces. Now, if 30 per cent of 
vacancies are there and if they are not recruiting men and officers and if they are not depending 
on themselves for this thing and all the time, for any incident happening, they are asking for 
Forces, we will definitely give, but holding the elections is also one of the responsibilities 
and if the Forces have to be given, they have to be given by the Union Government, not only 
the Union Government but we have brought the Forces from the State Government also in 
order to be deployed to man the elections also. So,  I think, it would be necessary for the 
State Governments to fill in the vacancies that they have. It will be necessary for them to use 
the Forces in the manner that they are put to the best use and it would be necessary for them 
to recruit more forces also. The Government of lndia will definitely help, but the Government 
of India cannot be asked not to give the Forces to the Election Commission when elections 
are to be held and not to withdraw the Forces from them. 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: The hon. Minister has already said that the 
Central Government does not have adequate Forces to  give protection to people. But, I 
think, the whole lndia knows that Assam is facing insurgency for so many years and so many 
people have died. Assam does not have adequate Forces and that is why they are asking for 
adequate Forces from the Central Government to give protection to people. Will the Central 
Government provide adequate Forces in Assam by increasing their Forces? He also said that 
whenever elections take place, they have to provide  security to States by shifting Forces. 
Will they stop shifting Forces so that terrorists d o not get into Assam and attack innocent 
people in Assam? It is very important. Will the Central Government give more importance 
to adequate Forces in Assam so that the people of Assam will have safety? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, I can understand the difficulty of Assam Government for 
that matter and it would be our endeavour to help them. But what is necessary is to deploy 
the Forces and use the Forces, which are given to them, in a manner in which they should be 
utilised. In Assam, we have not only the State Forces, but also about 60,000 policemen are 
there, nearly 20,000 policemen we have given them and then there are the Defence Forces 
also available working on the border areas. If they are not properly used and every time we 
ask as to why this has happened, the officer comes with a proposal that some more Forces 
should be asked from the Union Government. It becom es very difficult. The Union 
Government does not have Forces for regular services. They have reserve Forces. The Forces 
can be sent and they have to be withdrawn because, if required, they have to be sent to other 
places. I have full sympathy with the Assam Government. The Assam Government is facing 
a lot of difficulties. The Assam Government is facing the difficulties for the last so many

years, but that does not mean that we should shift the responsibility from the State Government 
to the Union Government and say that something has happened and Forces are not available. 
To provide Forces is the responsibility of the State Government and they should do it.

SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Sir, we are deeply distressed by the shocking killing of 
Hindi-speaking workers in Manipur yesterday, and, while strongly condemning the killings, 
I would ask the hon. Minister whether the Governmen t sees a more concerted attempt by 
different militant groups working in the North-East  to work together under more unified 
command targeting workers who have come from other parts of the country to the North-
East. And, if this is so, does the Government have a counter-strategy to meet this situation? 
I would also just like to ask whether the Government has any information as to who are the 
people involved in the dastardly killing of the workers.   . 
SHRI SHIVRAJ. V. PATIL: Sir, this is really a very important question. This has happened 
in Assam and we are indeed very, very sorry. Someti mes we feel ashamed of the things 
which happen in some parts of our country, and it i s necessary for us to take very strong 
action against those persons who are responsible. B ut, this is not happening in one State 
alone. This is happening in one or more North-Eastern States. It is happening in the South. It 
is happening in the West, and it is happening at many other places. It appears that there is a 
design to create this kind of problem in our country. In the name of language, this is being 
done. In the name of State, this is being done. In the name of religion, this is being done. In

the name of tribes this is being done. The intention is to see that these kinds of things happen 
and the country is disturbed; the State is disturbed, and the economic development, that we 
are trying to bring about, is also hampered, and then, so many other difficulties are created. 
What we are actually trying to do is that we have asked the State Governments to identify the 
areas where these kinds of things are likely to happen. Then, identify the persons, and then, 
you identify and anticipate the situation Before an ything happens, the action should be 
taken, We are also asking that they should increase the number of policemen, not in order to 
harass anybody but in order to protect the innocent persons. Enough number of policemen 
should be there. Then, there should be a transport facility provided. Supposing, something is 
happening at one place and if the forces are availa ble at some other place, they should be 
immediately transported without any delay to the pl ace where they are required. We are 
trying to do so many other things. You have rightly hit the nail on the head. This is really the 
question. This is not happening in one State but this is happening in many States about which 
we all are worried. We would like to certainly take steps. We have issued the directions. We 
have consulted the Chief Ministers, the Home Ministers and the DGs of the States. We are 
also instructing the police officers to be more correct. But this is mainly to be done by those 
who are actually in the field and if they are not sensitised on the issue in a proper manner, 
then, whatever we say here may not produce the results. We are asking them to bring this to 
their notice also and sensitise them.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Sir, the thrust of the question  is whether the Government is 
adopting the strategy, which has been proved succes sful in some other States, of enlisting 
the cooperation of the people, for fighting the pro blem of insurgency. I am afraid this 
question has not been answered by the hon. Minister . Nor has it been pressed through by 
other supplementary questions. Will the Minister accept the fact that the main effort of the 
Government has to be to get the support of the loca l people, of all political parties, and 
non-party persons, and their aim should be to spend  adequate amounts for getting the 
support of the people, for organising them into gro ups, for creating publicity material, and 
for holding meetings with support of the entire pop ulation in order to fight insurgency as a 
problem. 
Not just part (b) of the question, but, in fact, th is as a whole question has not been 
answered by the hon. Minister. Will he give an assurance on this now? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, this is a good question. In fact, part (a) of the question 
is more important than part (b) of the question. In  Punjab and Mizoram, insurgency or 
militancy, or, whatever you call it, was controlled . And I know how it was controlled. 
Probably, you were one of the persons who were dealing with it. The insurgency in Punjab 
was controlled not by using force, but by taking po litical decisions. I know that, in 
Punjab, the decision taken by the then Government w as to hold elections. When elections 
were held, the persons, who were in power, belongin g to the ruling party resigned. The 
elections were held and the power was transferred to the other party. It helped. 
In Mizoram also, the same thing happened. The Chief  Minister of the ruling party was 
asked to step down. When he stepped down, the Gover nment was given to the persons 
who were involved in these kinds of activities. The se two political decisions did help 
Punjab and Mizoram to bring about normalcy over there. This is one of the most important 
things. 
In fact, I thought that they would ask questions on  this. But instead of asking questions 
on this, they went to numbers. I was replying to th eir questions, and I was not replying to 
everything that is mentioned here. What you have as ked, in your question, is really 
correct. Without obtaining the cooperation of the p eople living in the villages, in the 
cities, in the rural areas, and in urban areas, it will not be very easy to control the 
situation. With bullets and with barrel of gun, it cannot be done so very easily. I would 
say that it is not impossible to do that, but the c ost of doing it will be very high. So, it will 
be necessary to have committees in the villages. It  will be necessary to have some people 
talking to them. When they were asked to talk to th em, some objections were raised in 
this House itself. Some people asked, "Why are you talking to them instead of using the 
gun?" When the talks did not help, then other metho ds were adopted. What you have said 
is really very correct. Some States have already ta ken steps to form committees in the 
villages, in the districts, in the mohallas, and al so in the cities. We are drafting a new 
Police Act in which we have said that this method a lso should be incorporated in the law 
and those people who are holding this responsibilit y and doing something over there, 
should be given some authority under the laws. 

16    Oral Answers ,   [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
NREGA knowledge network 
*288.      SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA:††  
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether to implement the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) in a 
better way, Government has created a mail group called NREGA knowledge network; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether most of the rural people are not aware of the various schemes of the Ministry 
and thus have remained unaware of the benefits of the various rural development schemes; 
and 
 if so, to what extent the creation of mail group wi ll create awareness amongst rural 
people about the various rural development schemes?  
THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table  of the House. 
Statement  
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Ministry of Rural Development has introduced e-knowledge network 
for effective implementation of NREGA. Innovations at worksites and local solutions are 
very helpful in meeting the challenges of implementation of NREGA across the country. E-
knowledge network helps in lateral transfer of thes e local solutions, especially among the 
District Programme Coordinators (DPCs). The knowledge network aims at connecting DPCs 
and providing solutions on demand through a knowled ge pool built up dynamically by 
exchange of information, ideas and best practices. 
 No, Sir. Awareness generation is the most important  tool for success of all rural 
development schemes. To ensure that more and more people get benefits under such schemes, 
Ministry of Rural Development has adopted five pronged strategy for all rural development 
programmes. These are (i) awareness generation, (ii) people's participation, (iii) transparency, 
(iv) accountability-social audit through Gram Sabha and (v) strict vigilance and monitoring. 
 E-knowledge network has been introduced for effective implementation of a demand 
based programme. As NREGA is demand based, knowledge network helps in meeting the 
challenges of its implementation across the country. Knowledge network aims at connecting 
the Disctrict Programme Coordinators who are responsible for implementation of NREGA 
in the districts. For other Rural Development Progr ammes of the Ministry, the website 
www.rural.nic.in  has detailed information. 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Sir, I would like to ask the hon. Minister that the 
purpose of the network was to share knowledge and experiences on NREGA so that the best 
practices could be used by other States as well. Sir, for instance, the State of Orissa has put 
into place a very effective MIS, management informa tion system, and also hired trained 
technical people to implement the system which has actually resulted in a much higher usage. 
So, Sir, the question that I would like to ask is: What are the significant lessons that have 
been learnt using this network and whether these experiences have been used by any other 
State to actually enrich or to make the scheme more effective? Does the Ministry have any 
details of other States that have shared and used the information? 
†† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA .

Revenue loss due to SEZs  
†*289. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:  
 whether it. is a fact that government is suffering loss of revenue worth more than one 
lakh crore rupees every year due to establishment of Special Economic Zones 
(SEZs); 
 if so, the details thereof and Government's point of view in this regard; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  

Oral Answers [19 MARCH 2008] to Questions   21 
 whether it is also a fact that the ministry of Finance and Ministry of Commerce differ 
in their opinion and attitude with reference to los s of revenue as a result of setting up of 
SEZs; and 
 if so, the reasons thereof and the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY 
OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
 No, Sir. 
 Does not arise. 
 and (d) In the Economic Survey for 2007-08 presente d to the Parliament, the 
Ministry of Finance has given facts relating to Spe cial Economic Zones which is as 
follows: 
"Exports from Special Economic Zones have been showing steady increase. As compared 
to exports of Rs. 22,480 crore made by SEZs in 2005 -06, exports to the tune of Rs. 
34,615 crore have been effected in the year 2006-07 , registering a growth of 52 per cent. 
Projected exports for 2007-08 from Special Economic Zones is Rs. 67088 crore. 
In the SEZs which have been set up/notified prior t o the coming into force of the SEZ 
Act, at present there are 1277 units in operation, providing direct employment to over 2 
lakh persons (about 40 per cent of whom are women).  Out of this, 36,463 persons are in 
the private/State Government SEZs, most of which had come up after February, 2006. The 
newly notified SEZs, which have come up after Febru ary 10, 2006, have provided direct 
employment to 61,015 persons. 
Private investments in the 19 SEZs which were set u p prior to coming into force of the 
SEZ Act 2005 is of the order of about Rs. 7104 cror e. Investment of the order of Rs. 
67,347 crore has already been made in the newly not ified SEZs which came up after 
February 10, 2006. 
Apprehensions have been expressed on misuse of the scheme and relocation of existing 
industries into SEZs. However, experience, has show n that these apprehensions are ill 
founded and fresh investments and employment have b een flowing into the Special 
Economic Zones. For example, Nokia Electronics hard ware SEZ in Sriperumbudur is 
already providing employment to 6637 persons, majority of whom are women. Hyderabad 
Gems SEZ has already employed 2000 persons after pr oviding training to them, out of 
which 1200 are girls. They have projected direct em ployment of about 30,000 persons. 
Apache SEZ being set up in Andhra Pradesh, is expec ted to employ 20,000 persons to 
manufacture 10,00,000 pairs of shoes every month. C urrent employment in Apache SEZ 
is 4500 persons. Brandix Apparels, a Sir Lankan FDI  project is expected to provide 
employment to 60,000 workers over a period of three  years. Even in the services sector 
12.5 million sq. metres space is expected to be cre ated in the 1T/ITES SEZs which is 
estimated to translate into 12.5 lakh jobs. The ben efits derived from multiplier effect of 
the investments and additional economic activity in  the SEZs along with the employment 
generated is estimated to far outweigh the revenue losses on account of tax exemptions 

22  Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
given to the SEZs. These SEZs are freshly developed  industrial clusters and are not 
relocated from elsewhere. 
Concerns have been expressed regarding acquisition of agricultural land for setting up 
SEZs. The State Governments have been advised by th e Centre that in case of land 
acquisition for Special Economic Zones, first prior ity should be for acquisition of waste 
and barren land and if necessary single crop agricu ltural land could be acquired for the 
SEZs. If perforce a portion of double cropped agric ultural land has to be acquired to meet 
the minimum area requirements, especially for multi product Special Economic Zones, the 
same should not exceed 10 per cent of the total lan d required for the SEZ. Various issues 
related to setting up of SEZs in the country, inclu ding issues raised by various political 
parties, have been addressed by the Empowered Group  of Ministers (EGOM). Pursuant to 
the decision taken by the EGOM, all State Governments have been informed that the Board 
of Approval will not approve any SEZs where the Sta te Governments have carried out or 
propose to carry out compulsory acquisiton of land for such SEZs after April 5, 2007." 
The views of the Department of Commerce are in agre ement with the above facts and 
hence the question of any difference of opinion does not arise.

Secretive purchase of land along Pakistan border in Rajasthan  
†*203.    SHRI AJAY MAROO: 
SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 whether Government's attention has been drawn to media reports in which it has been 
mentioned that the land of certain areas of Rajasthan along Pakistan border has been purchased 
by some unknown persons in a secretive manner; 
 if so, the information available with Government in this regard; and 
 the action taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. 
RADHIKA SELVI) (a) to (c) Government is aware that large scale land transactions over 
the last five years have taken place in the border areas of Rajasthan. The State Government

with the intention of identifying the purchasers an d ascertaining the motives behind such 
transactions. Preliminary enquiries indicate that lands have also been purchased by many 
parties from places other than Rajasthan. While spe culation linked to expectations about 
improved highway connectivity, new projects of irrigation and prospects of oil and gas finds 
may be a factor for accelerated investment in land in these areas, a definite conclusion/ 
analysis will be possible only after completion of the detailed enquiry being undertaken by 
the Government of Rajasthan with the support of the Central Government agencies. A high 
level review on the subject matter has also been held in the Ministry of Home affairs and the 
issue is being closely monitored in coordination wi th the State Government, from time to 
time.

Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) maintains record of industries in

other companies, relief and concessions in the form  of rescheduling of dues by Financial

*298.      SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:  
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) is covering 330 
districts from April, 2007, whether fool-proof modalities have been evolved to avoid any 
discrepancies pointed out in the CAG Report for period covering February, 2006-March, 
2007;and 
 as the Gram Panchayats have been actively involved in issuance of Job-Cards and 
giving work or compensation thereof to the eligible rural household, whether panchayats 
have been sensitized to extend positive support to help intended beneficiaries under this 
scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) Ministry of Rural Development had reque sted CAG to undertake 
performance audit of the implementation of NREGA in phase I districts for the year 
2006-07. Accordingly, CAG conducted audit in 68 districts of 26 States. CAG submitted 
its draft report on 17.12.2007 to the Ministry. The draft report has been examined in the 
Ministry and has also been shared with all the States. CAG has made a total of 1416 
findings in its draft report. These mainly relate to procedures such as application for 
employment, issue of dated receipts, job card formats, muster rolls, maintenance of 
record registers. In addition, 34 cases relate to financial matters. These are regarding 
instances of use of funds for non permissible activities/ineligible persons/agencies and 
incorrect accounting of expenditure. The States hav e given their responses to the 
observations made by CAG in the draft report. These have been sent to CAG. State 
responses are in the process of examination by CAG for finalisation of the performance 
audit report of NREGA.  
The government has evolved the following modalities to avoid the discrepancies pointed 
out in the draft CAG report.  
(1) Transparency  
(i) Payment of wages through workers accounts in Banks/post offices:  
 Instructions have been issued to state governments for coordination with the 
Department of Posts to ensure that accounts of NREGA workers are opened in 
Banks/Post offices for payment of wages and are made fully effective during 
2008-09.  
 Draft Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the State governments and 
Department of Post to ensure smooth payment to workers through their postal 
accounts is being finalised. 

Written Answers to [ 19 MARCH 2008] Starred Questions    33 
(c) Workers accounts in Banks/Post offices have been opened in some states. Andhra 
Pradesh, Jharkhand and karnataka have taken the lea d in this direction. Other 
states that have reported their progress so far are Bihar, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West 
Bengal and Madhya Pradesh. A total of 11028779 acco unts have so far been 
opened in these states. Remaining states are taking action in this regard. 
(ii) States have been advised to conduct social audit of each and every work of NREGA 
within three months. Social Audit has been done in 76000 Gram Panchayats. 
(iii) Citizen Information Board has been introduced. This board is to be displayed at all 
prominent places. This will enable the local commun ity to know the works being 
undertaken under NREGA and would also facilitate th e process of spreading 
awareness about the programme. 
(2) Generating Awareness  
Steps taken to generate awareness about NREGA are:  
(i) Initiatives taken by State Government: 
 Gram Sabhas and one day orientation of all Sarpanches at the Block level have 
been held.  
 Leaflets and brochures in local language are being provided. 
 Village camps have been organized by the District teams and Self-Help Groups 
are being associated in the awareness generation 
(ii) Action taken by the Central Government:  
 CAPART  has been asked to provide training to the NGOs and Civil Society 
organisations associated in the awareness generation campaign.  
 The Government of India has decided to introduce awards to be known as Rozgar 
Jagrookta Puraskar (Employment awareness awards) to recognize the outstanding 
contribution by the civil society organisations for promoting effective  
implementation of NREGA in different states of the country. 
 Use of media, TV spots, radio jingles, advertisements, films. 
 Development and dissemination of brochures and peoples primers. 
(3) Vigilance and monitoring  
(i) Implementation of NREG Act is monitored on regular basis. Vigilance and Monitoring 
Committees have been set up at State as well as dis trict levels. Local MPs are the 
members of the district Vigilance and Monitoring Committees. Village level Vigilance 
and Monitoring Committees have also been set up for local monitoring. Members of 
_the Central Employment Guarantee Council also unde rtake field visits to various 
districts. National Level Monitors and Area Officer s visit various districts to over 
see the progress of the Act. So far, NLMs have made 331 visits to Phase I and Phase 
II districts. 
(ii) Muster Roll verification has to be done in a campaign mode and consolidated reports 
sent to the Ministry. So far, 4621120 Muster rolls have been verified. 1126914 Muster 
rolls have been placed on the website.

(4) Regular Review of NREGA  
(i) Review with State Governments 
 During the year 2007-2008, three Regional Review Committee meetings have been 
held to cover review of all States. These were held  at Bhubaneswar (16-17 
September), Jaipur (24-25 September) and Guwahati (9-10 October). 
 Review meeting with State Secretaries (Rural Development) of all States was held 
on 18.12.07 in Delhi. 
 Meeting of the Performance review Committee was held in Delhi during 16-17 
January, 2008. 
 A meeting with State Secretaries (RD) of all States was held in Delhi in January, 2008 
to discuss the draft CAG report.

Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.

Progress of NREGA was reviewed in the interactive session with Members of Parliament held 
during 20th-23rd August, 2007 and 5th-6th September, 2007.

to Members of Parliament informing them about the status of implementation of the Act from time 
to time. Monthly progress report of NREGA in respect of the district of constituency of each

(i) A comprehensive Web-based MIS www.nrega.nic.in  has been implemented which

sanctioned shelf of works, work estimates, work in progress, measurement; Financial 
indicators like funds available/spent, amount paid as wages, materials and administrative 
expenses. Data software has been engineered for cross verification of records and for report 
generation. Details of 25001781 Job Cards and 1126914 Muster rolls have been placed on 
the website. 
(ii) Ministry of Rural Development has introduced e -knowledge network for effective 
implementation of NREGA. Innovations at worksites and local solutions are very helpful 
in meeting the challenges of implementation of NREG A across the country. E-
knowledge network helps in lateral transfer of these local solutions, especially among 
the District Programme Coordinators. The knowledge network aims at connecting 
practitioners and providing solutions on demand through a knowledge pool built up 
dynamically by exchange of information, ideas and best practices. 
(b) Yes, Sir. Gram Panchayats have been assigned a pivotal role in the implementation of 
NREGA. They are responsible for planning of works, registering households, issuing job cards, 
allocating employment, executing at least 50% of the works in terms of cost and monitoring the 
implementation of the scheme at the village level. Instructions have been issued to all States that 
one dedicated Gram Rojgar Sahayak(GRS) may be appointed in

2045. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state:  
 whether concerns of India alongwith Sourth Africa, Argentina and Brazil were ignored 
in Doha draft; 
 if so, the reaction of the Ministry thereto; and 
 what steps Government is taking to address core farm trade market access issues in 
the Doha trade negotiations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY 
OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (c) The Chair of 
the Committee on Agriculture (Special Session), which is the Negotiating Group on 
Agriculture of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), brought out Revised Draft Modalities 
for Agriculture on 8 February, 2008. This reflects the outcome of deliberations in the 
Negotiating Group on an earlier draft brought out by the Chair in July 2007. The draft 
modalities contain proposals on the three pillars of the Agriculture Negotiations, namely, 
domestic support, market access and export competition.  
While the revised draft reflects progress in some areas, it also contains new proposals on 
some issues, which would require detailed deliberations e.g. Special Products (SPs), the 
Special Safeguard Mechanism, the Special Agricultural Safeguard, Tropical Products, Tariff 
Simplification etc. There are also some other issues on which large divergences still exist, 
e.g. reductions in overall trade-distorting domestic support (OTDS), market access in 
Sensitive Products, Tariff Capping etc.  
India has been working closely with her coalition partners, including Sourth Africa, 
Argentina and Brazil, in developing country groupings in order to achieve an outcome that 
would fully reflect the level of ambition of the Doha mandate and the interests of developing 
countries. During the negotiations, India has made it clear that a substantial and effective 
reduction in domestic support and tariffs in agriculture by develped countries while enabling 
developing countries to protect and promote the interests of their low income and resource 
poor farmers is a priority for India in the negotiations.  
India is also a Member of the NAMA 11 coalition which includes Argentina, Brazil and 
South Africa. Draft modalities on Non Agricultural Market Access (relating to industrial 
tariff lines), were issue in July 2007 and had invited criticism from two-thirds of the WTO 
Membership. The revised draft modalities, which were brought out on 8 February 2008, do 
not meet the concerns of the NAMA 11 coalition and they have stated this during negotiation.

imprisonment, provided for the alleged offence, he should be released on his personal 
bond, with or without sureties. It also provides that in no case will an undertrial 
prisoner be detained beyound the maximum period of imprisonment for which he 
can be convicted for the alleged offence. Further, Section 436 (1) of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973 has also been amended to make a mandatory provision 
that if the arrested person is accused for a bailable offence and he is an indigent and 
cannot furnish surety, the Court shall release him on his execution of a bond without 
sureties. 
 The Government of India has introduced the system of plea bargainihg in 2006 
primarily to reduce pendency of cases in trial courts and overcrowding in prisons. 
 For disposal of long pending sessions and other cases, the Government of India has 
also set up 1562 Fast Track Courts.

RADHIKA SELVI): (a) and (b) 215 kms. fencing has so  far been completed as against 
310 km sanctioned, in Gujarat Sector, thereby, leaving a stretch of 95 kms. to be completed. 
The reasons for delay in completion of fencing work are as under:— 
(i) Peculiar unforeseen and unpredictable geographical conditions prevailing in the Rann 
of Kutch area. 
(ii) Keeping in view of the experiences of devastat ing earthquakes occurred on 26th 
January, 2001, severe floods and heavy rainfall in 2003 and unprecedented severe 
devastating flood in 2006, the recommendations of C entral Road Research 
Institute (CRRI) were obtained from time to time ba sed on which changes were 
made in the specification. This resulted in cost and time overrun. 
(iii) Works are implemented in far away locations involving higher cost of transportation 
of construction material and machinery. 
(iv) Due to unprecedented natural calamities higher  specifications were adopted. 
Additional drainage layer was provided in the emban kment, resulting in cost 
escalation. 
(v) Some sites are prone to more floods and, theref ore, embankment height was kept 
more, resulting in cost escalation. 
Action is being taken for early completion of prece dural formalities to commence the 
construction of remaining portion of fencing in Gujarat Sector, expeditiously. 
 As part of the pilot project of issue of Multi-purpose National Identity Card (MNIC), 
covering 12 States and 1 Union Territory, the Lakhpat taluk of Kutch district of Gujarat, has 
been included in the scheme. However, no decision h as been taken, so far, with respect to 
issue of identity cards to other border areas of Gujarat. In respect of intruders, they are dealt 
as per law of the land and the question of issue of  identity cards to the intruders, who are 
citizens of other countries does not arise.. 127 intruders were apprehended by the BSF 2005 
in the Gujarat sector. 
 Border Area Development Programme (BADP) is implemented in 361 border blocks 
of 96 districts covering 17 States. Various works such as construction of link roads, provisions 
of water pipeline to border villages for supply of drinking water, provision of electricity, 
construction of school building, hospitals, etc. ar e implemented under BADP for 
comprehensive development of border areas as well a s border population. An amount of 
Rs. 635 crore has been allocated for the BADP in the financial year 2008-09. Action has also 
been taken to implement various Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) and flagship schemes 
of Government of lndia in the border areas through the respective central ministries. 
As part of the comprehensive fencing work in the bo rders of India-Pakistan and India-
Bangladesh construction of roads are also taken up by the MHA. Further, as a special package, 
construction of roads along the India-China, India-Nepal and India-Bhutan are also proposed 
to be taken up by MHA. In addition, construction of  roads under the Central Scheme viz 
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) of Ministry of Rural Development are also 
being taken up.

 whether it is a fact that our Indian labour lacks competitiveness in world market;

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT

drivers, welders, fitters, machine operators coming from China and other countries.

working practices, safety norms and use of tools. The trainees are also given exposure on

Poor sanitation facilities in rural areas 
2155. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of RURAL  DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 whether rural sanitation continues to be a serious issue to be addressed by the 
Governments both at the Central and the States; 
 if so, the details thereof and the steps taken by G overnment thereon during the last 
three years; and 
 the reasons for continued poor sanitation facilities in rural areas of the country and the 
steps proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) The Government continues to give utmost 
importance in supplementing the efforts of the Stat e Governments to provide sanitation 
facilities to the rural masses. The scheme of Central Rural Sanitation Programme was revised 
in 1999 and "Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC)" launched. The programme has been continued 
in the XI Plan period and now scaled up to cover 582 rural districts of the country. During 
the last three years, the programme has been enhanced to include the component of solid and 
liquid waste management and provision of revolving fund to each district. To encourage the 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRI) to take up sanita tion promotion and attain 100% open 
defecation free environment, incentive scheme Nirma l Gram Puraskar (NGP) has been 
launched. During 2004-05, 39 PRIs from 6 States rec eived NGP. This number had further 
increased to 769 PRIs in 2006 and to 4959 PRIS in 2 007. Intensive monitoring, awareness 
and education campaigns, Capacity building activities are being taken up by each State to 
improve implementation. The Center has also enhanced the budget allocation for TSC in the 
last three years, from Rs. 400 crore in 2004-05 to Rs. 700 crore in 2005-06, Rs. 800 crore in 
2006-07 and Rs. 1060 crore in 2007-08. 
(c) The reason for poor sanitation is mainly the problem of open defecation, which was 
the only form of sanitation for the majority of the population in rural areas. This practice is 

134    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
prominently due to the traditional behavioral pattern and lack of awareness of the people 
about the associated health hazards. To tackle this issue, the Total Sanitation Campaign 
(TSC) has been restructured to a community led and people centered approach. The 
programme gives emphasis on Information, Education and Communication (IEC) for demand 
generation for sanitation facilities. It also lays emphasis on school sanitation and hygience 
education for bringing about attitudinal and behavioral changes for relevant sanitation and 
hygience practices from young age itself. The programme also develops convergence with 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and Sarva Sikhsha Abhiyan (SSA) for awareness 
creation and hygiene education among the people and children in the rural areas.

Statement  
Important measures taken by Government in recent pa st to help Indian textile sector  
(i) To improve productivity and quality of cotton f or manufacture and export of 
competitive downstream textile products, Government has launched the Technology 
Mission on Cotton (TMC). 
(ii) To facilitate the modernisation and upgradatio n of the textile industry both in the 
organised and unorganized sectors, Government has l aunched the Technology 
Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS). The Scheme has been  further fine tuned to 
increase the rapid investments in the targeted sub-sectors of the textile industry. The 
cost of machinery has been further brought down by reducing the customs duty on 
imports. 
(iii) To provide the textile industry with world-class infrastructure facilities for setting up 
their textile units meeting international environmental and social standards, a Public-
Private Partnership (PPP) based Scheme known as the "Scheme for Integrated Textile 
Park (SITP)" has been introduced in August 2005. 
(iv) In 2004-05 Budget, the entire textile sector, except for man-made fibre and filament 
yarn was provided optional exemption from excise duty. 
(v) Government has launched the Debt Restructuring Scheme w.e.f. Sept., 2003 with the 
principal objective to permit banks to lend to the textile sector at 8-9% rate of 
interest 
(vi) In order to cater to the growing skilled manpo wer requirements at shop floor level, 
Government is providing assistance for strengthenin g existing and opening new 
Apparel Training and Design Centres (ATDCs). 
(vii) Government has allowed 100% Foreign Direct Investment in the textile sector under 
automatic route. 
(viii) Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and knitwear from SSI 
sector so that large scale investments may be encouraged in these sectors. 
(ix) National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT ) has been set up to provide the 
leadership role in sensitizing the Industry to the concept of value addition by inducting 

Written Answers to [19 MARCH 2008] Unstarred Questions 151 
trained professionals to manage the industry. This has resulted in an increased demand for 
trained professionals in various sectors servicing the industry. 
(x) In order to promote the Technical textiles, Government has approved a Scheme, which 
aims at baseline survey of technical textiles units and for setting up of four Centres of 
Excellence, one each for Agrotech, Buildtech, Meditech and Geotech with the total 
outlay of Rs. 48 crore for 11th Plan period.

Crisis due to fall in price of Natural vanilla beans 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, I am raising a very urgent matter in 
the House which is related to the Vanilla farmers i n Kerala. Sir, the price of vanilla 
beans has reduced from Rs. 3,000 per kilogram to Rs . 30 per kilogram. As a 
result, the farmers are facing very acute crisis. I n order to save the farmers, there 
was a demand to ban the synthetic vanilla, and to i ntroduce natural vanilla flavour 
for ice-cream manufacturing. Recently, Sir, Amul, t he Cooperative Milk 
Manufacturing Society from Gujarat has taken a deci sion that in order to save the 
vanilla beans farmers, henceforth, they are going t o use natural vanilla flavour in 
its entire range of vanilla ice-creams. It is a goo d step taken by Amul. So, I would 
urge upon the Government that it should also take a decision making use of natural 
vanilla in ice-cream mandatory all over India. Sir,  use of natural vanilla should be 
made mandatory for all the manufacturers of ice cre am. The manufacturers 
should switch over from synthetic vanilla to natural vanilla. The Government has to 
take a decision in this regard. The peasants and agriculturists are demanding this. 
The Government has to take a decision. I would urge that upon that on the basis of 
the decision of Amul the Government should also tak e a decision in this regard as 
early as possible of switching over from synthetic vanilla to natural vanilla in order to 
help the farmers a little bit. I urge upon the Government to take an urgent decision 
in this regard. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura): Sir, I associate mys elf with the veiws 
expressed by the hon. Member. 
SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Sir, I also assoc iate myself with the 
views expressed by the hon. Member. 
PROF. P.J. KURIEN (Kerala): Sir, I also associate m yself with the views 
expressed by the hon. Member. Synthetic vanilla is not good for health.

Need to address problems of children 
suffering from dyslexia 
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE (Maharashtra): Sir, 1 stand h ere with anguish to 
share in this august House and to all my esteemed colleagues about a suicide by a 
21 year old today, whose name is Swhetabh Nagar, who is a dyslexic child. He was 
21 years old and not a child. But it is more about education. I think, a lot has been 
discussed in the other House about the suicides of normal children. But, I think, 
disabilities have to be addressed through Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. The hon. 
Finance Minister has also mentioned in his speech that our focus on enrolment has 
to move to the quality of education. So, I urge the  House to bring up the issue of 
various disabilities because I don't think half the  parents even know their children 
are dyslexic or discalculiar. These are all disabil ities which cannot be solved only 
by the elite schools and this issue is not going to  be solved by counsellors but by 
training the teachers. So, I urge the Government to  take some serious 
cognisance of all these children. We talk about inc lusion of this in Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan but there are no results in this field. So, 1 urge the Ministry to take serious 
cognisance of all these disabilities of children who are 100 per cent normal but have 
some learning disabilities and there is need for mo re teacher training institutes 
which are focussed on this issue. Thank you.

SPECIAL MENTIONS  
Demand to take urgent measures to improve market hare 
of Life Insurance Corporation  
SHRI M. V. MYSURA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the LIC was the leading 
life insurance company with 88 per cent market shar e, 21 crore policyholders and 
with about Rs. 1.3 lakh crore of renewal premium till 2004. But, unfortunately, due to 
unilateral decisions taken by LIC, its market share dwindled to 64 per cent in 2007 
and its investment in infrastructure and social sec tor projects came down from 
Rs. 45,000 crores in 2003 to Rs. 40,000 Crores in 2 007. 
One of the major reasons behind this is unilateral implementation of GOIBS 
2004. This move demoralised and de-motivated the De velopment Officers who 
are considered as the backbone of LIC. In 2003-04, Development Officers paid 1.3 
per cent as marketing expenses and incentives and i n 2006-07 it came down to 
0.75 per cent in spite of double in premium collections which stood at Rs. 1.3 lakh 
crores. 
Other decisions taken by LIC against the interest o f policyholders is its 90 per 
cent investment in ULIPs which lack security and ar e stock market-oriented 
investment plans. Here, the risk is shifted on to p olicyholders, unlike in 
conventional policies. Now, LIC is doing only 10 per cent insurance plans. 
Thirdly, LIC is now outsourcing services by appointing corporate agents, referral 
agencies, finance executives by paying more money. Now, I understand that LIC 
has brought out another GOIBS, 2007 for unilateral implementation without any 
discussion with the Development Officers, agents, etc. 
In view of this, I request the Government of India to immediately direct LIC to 
revamp GOIBS, 2007 and revert back to pre-GOIBS, 20 04 status and pay 
Development Officers as per MOU and desist itself from investing in ULIPs to save 
LIC from its downfall.

Demand for formation of farmers' club to impart knowledge about crop 
pattern, soiland weather condition  
SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I congrat ulate the UPA 
Government for launching several schemes including a loan waiver of Rs. 60,000 
Crores for farmers. The farmers' suffering is due to several factors, namely, lack of 
remunerative prices for agricultural commodities, high cost of cultivation, lack of 
storage facilities to enable them to keep the produ ce and sell when prices go up, 
scarcity of water, failure to find water when the well/ bore-well are dug, inter crops 
damaged due to unexpected rain, crop failure, etc. Unless a practical input is 
obtained, not from the experts but from farmers wor king at the ground-level, the 
reality cannot be understood and problems cannot be solved. Due to various land 
ceiling laws, the holdings have diminished. It is n ecessary to club these small 
holdings into one block and the Government must help the cultivation by digging a 
borewell in one place and distribute the water in turn system and lend the modern 
machineries to farmers and recover the money as a land revenue later. In this way, 
the Government also will get back the invested mone y, in which case, there is no 
need for subsidy and loan waiver etc. Involvement of IT technology in every village by 
connecting the computers to the field and field to market, will go long way in 
redressing the suffering of the farmers. Formation of farmers' club, imparting 
knowledge about the crop pattern, soil and weather conditions, ground water 
position are necessary. This will help the farmers tremendously. I urge the 
Government of India to expeditiously work in this d irection without any loss of 
time. 
Demand to take steps for interlinking of rivers in the country 
SHRIMATI KANIMOZHI (Tamil Nadu): Sir, the Governmen t of Tamil Nadu had 
submitted certain issues regarding interlinking of rivers and gave some suggestions, 
namely, (i) to convene a meeting of the Chief Ministers concerned for interlinking of 
the Peninsular Rivers, (ii) to take immediate steps  to include interlinking of rivers 
in the Eleventh Plan, and, (iii) to ensure that int erlinking of the Peninsular Rivers 
is specifically included and funded in the Eleventh Five Year Plan. 
Sir, in this regard, the Chief Minister also commun icated to the hon. Prime 
Minister on 6th September, 2006 and again reminded him on 7th January, 2007. 
The Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, drawing the attention of the Prime Minister on 
the National Water Policy 2002, rightly emphasized that the water should be made 
available to water-starved areas by transfer from o ther areas, including transfer 
from one river basin to another, based on a nationa l perspective and after taking 
into account the areas and the basins. 
Further the Chief Minister pleaded to ensure that i nterlinking of the Peninsular 
Rivers is specially included and funded in the Elev enth Five Year Plan on the 
basis of the NDC deliberations. As these proposals are important, whether these 
have been included in the Eleventh Five Year Plan, which has been approved 
recently. As the issues are important, which will help not only Tamil Nadu but other 
States also, I urge upon the Government to take final decision on these issues.

Concern over the problem of waterlogging in Faridkot , Muktesar and Ferozepur  
district of Punjab  
SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA (Punjab): Sir, I take this opportunity to draw the 
attention of the Minister of Water Resources of the Central Government to the serious problem 
of waterlogging and salination in three district of Punjab, namely, Faridkot, Muktesar and 
Ferozepur. The problem has been caused by excessive seepage of water from Rajasthan 
Feeder, which is an inter-State canal and Sirhind Feeder — a State canal. Waterlogging 
has not only adversely affected the soil of the area but has also affected the health of 
large number of population living there. The cases of cancer have recently been reported 
in the area. 
To tackle the problem of waterlogging in the State, the State Government has worked out 
two projects — one for the re-lining of Rajasthan Feeder, which is an inter-State canal. Its 
cost works out to be Rs. 425 crore, for which the Central Government has to bear 90 per cent 
cost. The other project is for the re-lining of the Sirhind Feeder, which is a State canal and its 
cost of Rs. 225 crore. As this project is vital not only to the State but also to the nation, the 
Central Govenment is requested to give a liberal assistance for the same. 
As both these projects have to be implemented on a priority basis, the Central Government 
is requested to expedite their share of the costs to the State Government. 
Request to withdraw restriction of mandatory sixty per cent marks for availing

students belonging to SC/ST community. The scheme of providing scholarships to 
SC/ST students had been initiated to provide financial assistance for pursuing higher 
studies to those students who are socially and fina ncially weak. But, the Central 
Government's decision of imposing restriction of si xty per cent marks being made 
compulsory for SC students to become eligible for s eeking scholarship is totally

Concern over the adverse impact of Global Economic Recession on 
Indian Economy  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, I rise to commend the attention of 
the House over the possible spectre of global econo my that may adversely impact 
country's economic growth . Continuous increase in international oil prices in recent 
week and concomitant hardening of US Dollar against Rupee as against broader global 
trend towards weaker Dollar against other currencies, has had definite impact on our 
domestic economy. The recent CSO figures indicate a significant dip in the industrial 
growth rate. Manufacturing sector has slowed down significantly. Mining and electricity 
generation sector too have slowed down. The inflationary trend may precipitate further if 
there is a possible fall in global food stocks as per the assessments made by FAO. It 
has been predicted that the global consumption of w heat and rice will continue to 
outstrip production. The global wheat stocks were down to 107 million MT in 2007. 
Rice stocks came down to only 71 million MT in 2007 . The droughts in Australia, 
lower production in Ukraine and freeze in US have c ontributed to depleting global 
food stocks. With domestic production almost stagnating, such shortage of foodgrain 
can spark speculative trends as is evident in growing futures' prices in global markets 
I ask the Government to take necessary steps to build adequate food stocks to provide 
food security to our people. The Government must make support prices competitive 
in an open market to prevent unwarranted export of foodgrain thereby creating scarcity 
domestically, and inter alia, forcing the Government to import from global markets at 
much higher prices. Thank you. 
Need to take special measurs for increasing wheat production  
MS. MABEL REBELLO (Jharkhand): Sir, the great wheat panic of 2007 saw the global 
prices shot up by over 92 per cent during the year. Rice and corn prices also rose as 
sharply. FAO has declared that 854 million people go hungry around the world. Things are 
expected to get worse in 2008. 
Is mankind peering down an abyss of hunger? 
The global consumption of wheat and rice has outstripped their production for the past 
seven years running except in 2004-05. Production is growing, but the population is growing 
faster than that. 

174    Government [RAJYA SABHA]                                    Bills  
The global wheat stocks were down to 107 million MT in 2007 compared with over 
197 million MT in 2001; rice stocks were just 71 million MT compared with 136 million MT. 
All this means that the future supply of both wheat and rice is becoming more uncertain. That 
means prices are likely to keep going up. 
India stands at a tipping point, especially, as foodgrain production is stagnating. Wheat 
output was 72.8 million MT in 2002. This year, it is estimated at about 90 million MT. 
Meanwhile, population has increased to ,113 crore. So, there will be a need for imports. This, 
in turn, will fuel the global prices. Grain economist Mike Woolverton of Kansas State 
University said that as soon as India bought 7,95,000 MT of wheat at a record price of 
$389.45 in 8/2007, wheat futures in Europe rose by 70 per cent on expectations of more 
orders. 
A country which has 70 per cent people living below Rs. 20/- a day, will not have the 
puchasing capacity of wheat at these exorbitant prices. Hence, the country needs to produce 
more wheat by increasing irrigation, particularly, in States like Jharkhand, Orissa and Assam 
that have ideal wheat-producing climate. I would urge the Government to undertake special 
measures in these States to increase wheat production.
